summary: Discusses when it is appropriate to register and use an Autonomous System, and lists criteria for doing so. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: An Autonomous System (AS) is a group of IP prefixes that follow one clearly defined routing policy. RFC 1930 explains when a site needs a distinct AS and when it can use its provider's AS instead.

subtitle: Guidance on when a network's routing policy needs its own Autonomous System number.

tldr.problem: Operators were requesting Autonomous System numbers as a routine part of Internet connectivity, even when a separate routing policy did not require one. The number space is finite.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1930 defines an AS around a single, clearly defined routing policy and gives criteria and sample cases for deciding whether a network needs a separate AS.
tldr.outcome: The RFC's central guidance is to use a separate AS when routing policy differs from neighboring providers, especially for a multi-homed site. RFC 1930 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 6996 and RFC 7300.

today: RFC 1930 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 6) that has been updated by RFC 6996 and RFC 7300. The AS-number counts and 16-bit space described here reflect the RFC's publication period.

sections.title: Why the AS Guidelines Were Written
sections.content:
RFC 1930 is guidance for network operators and service providers deciding whether to create and register an Autonomous System. It was written to address confusion about how ASes should be used and to serve as a guide to exterior routing.

The RFC describes an AS as a unit of routing policy used by exterior routing protocols. It notes that BGP was the current de facto standard for inter-AS routing when the document was written.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC helps operators decide whether their network needs its own AS number. Its key question is whether the network has a routing policy that needs to be represented separately.

sections.title: An AS Represents One Routing Policy
sections.content:
The RFC defines an AS as a connected group of one or more IP prefixes, run by one or more operators, with a single and clearly defined routing policy. A prefix is a block of IP networks written as an address and mask, such as a CIDR block.

Routing policy governs the exchange of route information between ASes. For traffic to reach a prefix, one AS must announce the route and another must accept and use it. Each AS has a globally unique AS number that identifies it in routing exchanges.

Traffic in the two directions can take different paths, which the RFC calls asymmetric routing. It says this is not inherently bad but should be used with caution because it can cause performance problems for higher-level protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: An AS groups prefixes that follow the same routing policy. Its number identifies that policy group to neighboring networks.

sections.title: When a Separate AS Is Needed
sections.content:
Exchanging external routing information requires an AS, but that fact alone does not mean a site needs its own AS. The RFC advises putting as many prefixes as possible in one AS when they follow the same policy. A separate AS is needed when the site's routing policy differs from that of its border-gateway peers.

A single-homed site with one prefix or multiple prefixes generally does not need a separate AS; the prefixes can be placed in the provider's AS. A site connected to more than one service provider, each with its own routing policy, is the RFC's main example of a case requiring its own AS.

The RFC cautions against creating an AS merely for administrative grouping, one per classful network, or as preparation for a possible future provider. It says a policy difference may occasionally justify a separate AS for a single-homed site, but describes that as rare.
sections.plainLanguage: A site generally needs its own AS when it must express a routing policy different from its provider's. A single-homed site following its provider's policy usually does not need a separate one.

sections.title: The RFC's Sample Cases
sections.content:
The RFC compares three situations. A single-homed site with one prefix does not need a separate AS, and neither does a single-homed site with multiple prefixes, if the prefixes follow the provider's policy. In both cases the prefixes can be part of the provider's AS.

A multi-homed site, as defined in the RFC, connects to more than one service provider with separate routing policies. The RFC says it requires an AS distinct from those providers so that the site can represent its own policy and preferences. The site also needs facilities to run appropriate routing protocols, such as BGP4.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples distinguish single-homed sites from sites connected to providers with different policies. The multi-homed case is the RFC's main reason for a site to use its own AS.

sections.title: Prefix Origins and Internal Router Tags
sections.content:
The RFC says a prefix should generally belong to one origin AS, since there should be one routing policy for traffic destined for that prefix at each point in the Internet. Aggregation can make a prefix appear in more than one AS, but the document treats this as an exception.

Some router implementations use an AS number as an identifier for interior routing processes. The RFC says this internal tag need not be globally unique and is not visible to exterior routing protocols. Merely running an interior gateway protocol is not a reason to register an AS number.
sections.plainLanguage: A prefix should normally have one origin AS so its routing policy is clear. An internal router label does not need its own globally registered AS number.

sections.title: Number Space and Private Use
sections.content:
At the time RFC 1930 was written, AS numbers were 16-bit values, with 65535 unique numbers. It reported that some 5,100 ASes had been allocated and a little under 600 were actively routed in the global Internet. These counts and the number-space description are a snapshot from the RFC's publication period.

The RFC records the private-use range as 64512 through 65535 and says those numbers are not to be advertised on the global Internet. Its conclusion was that following the allocation criteria posed no immediate danger of exhaustion at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's number-space figures describe the situation when it was written. It sets aside a block for private use and says those numbers should not be announced on the global Internet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC identifies few security concerns related to selecting ASes. It notes that mappings between AS numbers and their owners are public in WHOIS and argues that hiding them would confuse people routing IP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The document treats AS selection as having few security concerns. It says AS-to-owner mappings are public and should remain understandable to people who route traffic.
